newsitem.title: NORWAY: Fierce battle seen in Statoil sale.
newsitem.headline: Fierce battle seen in Statoil sale.

text.p: Oil companies are expected to fiercely contest a battle for assets on the Norwegian continental shelf offered out by Den norske stats oljeselskap (Statoil) as part of a restructuring programme of its core activities, industry analysts Wood Mackenzie said on Monday.
The state Norwegian oil company announced in November that it had initiated a programme of buying, selling and swapping acreage to restructure its portfolio of upstream assets off Norway.

"Given the the desire for quality assets in Norway, we anticipate fierce competition for Statoil's interests in the prime Draugen and Njord developments off mid Norway," Wood Mackenzie said in a report. "Other assets in the Central North Sea could prove atractive to niche players," they said.
Statoil proposes to concentrate activities on five core areas, which hold the bulk of its commercial and technical reserves and from where it produces around 90 percent of its equity crude.
The plans mean that Statoil is willing to divest interests in 34 licences, including its equity stakes in several fields such as Njord and Draugen.

"At this stage the realignment of its domestic portfolio is Statoil's main aim. However, the company realises that the proposed reshuffle in Norway could provide it with the opportunity to undertake a number of international deals/swaps which could advance its longer term goals," Wood Mackenzie said.

They said Statoil had invited a number of companies to develop swap transactions based on the relevance of their portfolios to Statoil's intentions. Each company had received a "wish list" detailing which assets Statoil finds attractive.
Wood Mackenzie said the lists included assets primarily in Norway, but also on the British continental shelf and the Gulf of Mexico.

"Statoil has initiated what could be the largest asset sale in the North Sea in recent years...The combined base asset value of the commercial reserves, which are on offer, is in excess of $600 million," the report said.

It said that as well as focusing its portfolio Statoil's programme also addressed several other issues, such as rapidly declining oil production, limited portfolio of upcoming developments, lack of an international portfolio to balance its domestic interests and increasing exposure to potentially weaker gas prices through a swing towards gas rather than oil in Norway.
